subject: Climate & Environment
title: How Much Food We Waste
description: A micro-lesson that makes How Much Food We Waste usable.

hook.text: One-third of all food produced globally is lost or wasted. That's 1.3 billion tons per year.

buildup.text: In rich countries, most waste happens at retail and in homes — food tossed uneaten.

discovery.text: In poor countries, food is lost before it reaches the table — spoiled in storage or transit.

twist.text: If food waste were a country, it would be the third-largest greenhouse gas emitter on Earth.

climax.text: We produce enough food to feed 10 billion people. Distribution and waste are the real problems.

punchline.text: The world isn't short on food. It's short on respect for it.

quiz.question: What fraction of global food production is lost or wasted?

details.summary: Roughly one-third of all food produced globally is wasted, amounting to about 1.3 billion tonnes per year. In wealthy countries, most waste occurs at the retail and consumer level, while in developing nations it happens during harvest, storage, and transport due to infrastructure limitations.
details.whyItMatters: Food waste squanders the water, energy, land, and labor used in production and generates enormous greenhouse gas emissions. Reducing it is one of the most impactful climate actions available.
takeaways: About one-third of global food production is wasted annually
Food waste in landfills generates significant methane emissions
Wealthy nations waste most food at the consumer level

faq.question: How much greenhouse gas does food waste produce?
faq.answer: If food waste were a country, it would be the third-largest emitter of greenhouse gases after the US and China. Rotting food in landfills produces methane, and the wasted resources embedded in growing, transporting, and refrigerating uneaten food add significantly more.

faq.question: Why do wealthy countries waste so much food?
faq.answer: Abundance, aesthetic standards that reject imperfect produce, confusing date labels, large portion sizes, and low food costs relative to income all contribute. Consumers in wealthy countries waste more per capita because the financial motivation to avoid waste is weak.
